linebackers. Bring the same two players onto a 4-3 team and they would be listed as defensive ends, and
the identical alignment would be called a 4-2-5.

### 3-3-5: three meanings

The [**3-3-5**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-3-5) is three down linemen, three linebackers and
five defensive backs, and it is the one name in this section that means different things depending on
who says it.

- **When an NFL coach calls a 3-3-5 front,** he means a five-man line in nickel: three linemen inside, a
  stand-up edge on each end, and one linebacker behind them. The tite of @fig-tite-inside-zone is exactly
  this, the 3-4 team's nickel with its nose back on the field. It is the light-box run front of the Fangio
  tree, and the Staley branch of that tree calls it **Penny**, a nickel with a nose.[^penny]
- **When the roster count says 3-3-5,** it usually means something else: a four-man line with one edge
  listed as a defensive end and the other as a linebacker. That is what most of the 3-3-5 snaps in the
  data below are.
- **In college, "3-3-5" usually means the *3-3-5 stack*,** a different defense with three linemen and
  three linebackers stacked directly behind them, usually credited to Joe Lee Dunn at Memphis in 1991
  and spread in the 1990s as a way to put more speed on the field against spread offenses.[^stack] It
  belongs to [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

Which one you are looking at, the hands will tell you: three down inside the tackles with an edge on
each side is the coach's 3-3-5; four men on the line is the roster's.

### The labels, measured

You can see how loosely these names attach to the football in the play-by-play data. Since 2023, the
nflverse participation file (charted by FTN) lists the roster position of every defender on every snap,
so each snap's personnel can be counted as linemen–linebackers–defensive backs. Here is every 2025
nickel snap, split by what the roster labels call it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nickel-labels
#| fig-cap: "What each team's nickel snaps are called, if you count roster positions: 2025 regular season, every run and pass play with five defensive backs, by defense. Blue: four defensive linemen and two linebackers (4-2-5). Orange: three and three (3-3-5). Green: two and four (2-4-5). The league splits into two camps that line up almost identically on the field: teams whose edge rushers are listed as defensive ends (mostly 4-2-5, top) and teams whose edge rushers are listed as outside linebackers (mostly 2-4-5, bottom), with a few in between whose two edges carry one label each (3-3-5). Grey is everything else, about 3 percent of the league's nickel snaps: mostly 1-5-5 and 5-1-5 counts, plus a handful of snaps with a defender listed at an offensive position. The table below the chart shows that the three labels have the same box count and the same pass rush. Data: nflverse participation (FTN charting) joined to play-by-play via nflreadpy; positions are as FTN lists them, which follows team rosters."
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp
from IPython.display import Markdown

style.apply()


def split_personnel(s):
    """(DL, LB, DB) counts from an FTN-era string such as '3 CB, 2 DE, 2 DT, 1 FS, 1 MLB, 1 OLB, 1 SS'."""
    c = {}
    for v, k in re.findall(r"(\d+)\s+([A-Z]+)", str(s)):
        c[k] = c.get(k, 0) + int(v)
    dl = sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in ("DE", "DT", "NT", "DL"))
    lb = sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in ("OLB", "ILB", "MLB", "LB"))
    db = sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in ("CB", "FS", "SS", "S", "DB"))
    return dl, lb, db


part = nfl().load_participation([2025]).to_pandas()[
    ["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "defense_personnel", "defenders_in_box", "number_of_pass_rushers"]]
pb = pbp(2025, columns=["game_id", "play_id", "season_type", "play_type", "down", "defteam"])
pb = pb[(pb.season_type == "REG") & pb.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & pb.down.notna()]
snaps = pb.merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])
snaps = snaps[snaps.defense_personnel.notna()].copy()
cnt = snaps.defense_personnel.map(split_personnel)
snaps["dl"], snaps["lb"], snaps["db"] = [c[0] for c in cnt], [c[1] for c in cnt], [c[2] for c in cnt]
snaps = snaps[snaps.dl + snaps.lb + snaps.db == 11]
snaps["label"] = snaps.dl.astype(str) + "-" + snaps.lb.astype(str) + "-" + snaps.db.astype(str)
NICKEL_SHARE = (snaps.db == 5).mean()
BASE_SHARE = (snaps.db == 4).mean()
nk = snaps[snaps.db == 5]
LABELS = ["4-2-5", "3-3-5", "2-4-5"]
share = nk.groupby("defteam").label.value_counts(normalize=True).unstack(fill_value=0.0)
share = share.reindex(columns=LABELS, fill_value=0.0)
share["other"] = 1 - share[LABELS].sum(axis=1)
share = share.sort_values(["2-4-5", "3-3-5"], ascending=[True, True])
league = nk.label.value_counts(normalize=True)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 6.4))
colors = {"4-2-5": style.SERIES[0], "3-3-5": style.SERIES[1], "2-4-5": style.SERIES[2], "other": style.GRID}
left = np.zeros(len(share))
ys = np.arange(len(share))
for lab in LABELS + ["other"]:
    ax.barh(ys, share[lab].values * 100, left=left, color=colors[lab], height=0.72, edgecolor=style.SURFACE,
            linewidth=1.2, label=lab if lab != "other" else "other / unlisted")
    left += share[lab].values * 100
ax.set_yticks(ys)
ax.set_yticklabels(share.index, fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("share of the team's nickel snaps (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_title("2025 nickel snaps by roster label: same front, two names", fontsize=10)
ax.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.13), ncol=4, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (box count and pass rush by nickel label)"
def as_markdown(df):
    """A small table as a Markdown pipe table, which prints cleanly in every format."""
    cols = list(df.columns)
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(cols) + " |", "|" + "|".join([":--"] + ["--:"] * (len(cols) - 1)) + "|"]
    rows += ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in r) + " |" for r in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    return Markdown("\n".join(rows))


rows = []
for lab in LABELS:
    g = nk[nk.label == lab]
    passes = g[(g.play_type == "pass") & (g.number_of_pass_rushers > 0)]
    rows.append({"roster label": lab,
                 "share of nickel snaps": f"{len(g) / len(nk):.0%}",
                 "avg. defenders in the box": f"{g[g.defenders_in_box > 0].defenders_in_box.mean():.1f}",
                 "avg. pass rushers": f"{passes.number_of_pass_rushers.mean():.1f}",
                 "four-man rushes": f"{(passes.number_of_pass_rushers == 4).mean():.0%}"})
as_markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

Two things jump out of @fig-nickel-labels and the table under it. First, the league splits cleanly into
two camps, and the split has nothing to do with what the defenses do: it is about how teams list their
edge rushers. Teams whose edges are "defensive ends" play the 4-2-5; teams whose edges are "outside
linebackers" play the 2-4-5. Second, the three labels describe nearly identical football. All three put
about six defenders in the box, all three rush about four on passes, roughly three times in four exactly four.

That is why this book, and every coach you will read, asks you to **count hands, not names.** Before
the snap, count the players with a hand on the ground and the players standing at the ends of the line,
and note where the man nearest the center is. Four down is a four-man line, whatever the graphic says.
Two down with two standing edges is a four-man line too, built from 3-4 personnel. Three down inside
the tackles with an edge on each side is a tite, five on the line. The personnel label tells you which
players are on the field, which matters for what they *can* do (a 3-4 outside linebacker can drop into
coverage more comfortably than a 4-3 end); the alignment tells you what they are *about* to do.

## Multiple defenses: one personnel group, many fronts

If the label is personnel and the front is alignment, nothing stops a defense from playing several
fronts with the same eleven players. Almost every NFL defense now does. A
[**multiple defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-multiple-defense) (also called a
[**hybrid defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hybrid-defense)) lines up in more than one front
family, odd and even, four-man and five-man, often from the same personnel and sometimes switching
between them before the snap. "Now every team is 'multiple,'" one analyst wrote more than a decade
ago, and it has only become more true.[^multiple]

Belichick's Patriots were the model of the idea: a defense that might be a two-gap 3-4 one week and a
four-man front the next, built to take away whatever the opponent did best. The modern versions go
further, changing fronts *within* a series, and the most effective way to do it is a shift: show the
offense one front, then move into another as the quarterback is calling the protection.

```{python}
#| label: fig-same-personnel-two-fronts
#| fig-cap: "Same eleven players, two fronts (simulated; dark dots are hands on the ground; each lineman's label is his technique, and it changes when he moves). The defense is in 4-2-5 nickel personnel (four defensive linemen) against a shotgun one-back set with the tight end (Y) attached on the right. 1: it shows a four-man even front: four hands down, a wide 5 on the left, a 3, a 1, and a 5 on the right tackle, with the Mike and Will behind them. 2: as the quarterback calls his protection, the front shifts. The 1 slides onto the center; the 3 and the right end both slide to 4is, the end keeping his hand down; the left end (ringed) stands up and widens: the edge who changes stance. The Mike (ringed) walks up outside the tight end. 3: at the snap, five on the line, three hands down, all three inside the tackles: a tite, and every interior spot is still held by a defensive lineman. 4: the offense passes. Four rush (the three linemen and the standing left edge), and the walked-up Mike drops into the flat: a front that showed five on the line rushed four, and the player who looked like a rusher is in coverage."
def shift_play():
    off = gun11(y_attached=True)
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "5"), D("L3", "DL", 1.0, T("3", -1), "3"), D("R1", "DL", 1.0, T("1", 1), "1"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", 1), "5"),
           D("WILL", "LB", 4.7, -1.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 2.0, "M")] + secondary(nickel_w=-6.2, high=11.0,
                                                                                         safety_w=7.6)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    # the shift (Georgia's move into mint): the 1 to the nose, the 3 out to a 4i, the right end down to a 4i
    # with his hand still down, the left end stands up and widens; the Mike walks up outside the tight end
    go_to(p, "R1", (1.0, 0.0), "motion", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "L3", (1.0, T("4i", -1)), "motion", speed=0.2)
    go_to(p, "RE", (1.0, T("4i", 1)), "motion", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "LE", (1.0, -5.6), "motion", speed=0.4)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (1.0, 6.1), "motion", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (4.7, 0.6), "motion", speed=1.4)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (7.0, -14.7), "motion", speed=0.1)        # (keeps the clock running: a still opening frame)
    # after the snap: pass protection and a four-man rush; the walked-up Mike drops to the flat
    p.dropback(1.5)
    for k, end in [("LT", (-1.6, -3.6)), ("LG", (-1.4, -1.6)), ("C", (-1.3, 0.0)), ("RG", (-1.4, 1.6)),
                   ("RT", (-1.6, 3.4)), ("Y", (-1.3, 5.6))]:
        go_to(p, k, end, speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "LE", (-2.4, -4.9), "path", speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "L3", (-0.15, -2.4), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "R1", (-0.1, 0.1), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "RE", (-0.15, 2.5), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.0, 9.4), "path", speed=5.6)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (7.0, 0.4), "path", speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (6.0, -7.6), "path", speed=3.0)
    for k, r_ in [("H", (6.0, -9.6)), ("Z", (8.0, 15.0)), ("X", (8.0, -15.0))]:
        go_to(p, k, r_, "path", speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.3, 2.1), "path", speed=3.0)
    return p


P_SHIFT = shift_play()
_KF = P_SHIFT._compile()[0]
_HALF = {k: float(_KF[k][0, 0]) / 2 for k in ("LE", "L3", "R1", "RE")}     # half-way through each man's shift
_NEW = {"LE": "E", "L3": "4i", "R1": "0", "RE": "4i"}


def shift_label(key, t):
    """Technique labels follow the shift: each lineman takes his new number half-way through his move."""
    return _NEW[key] if key in _NEW and t >= _HALF[key] else None


def shift_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    keys = ["L3", "R1", "RE"] + (["LE"] if t < _HALF["LE"] else [])
    hands(fld, play, keys, t=t, half=0.57)


t0 = min(float(f[0, 0]) for f in _KF.values())
animation_or_strip([(P_SHIFT, round(t0 + 0.4, 1), ""), (P_SHIFT, -0.7, ""), (P_SHIFT, 0.0, ""),
                    (P_SHIFT, 1.1, "")],
                   notes=["shows a four-man line:\nfour hands down",
                          "the shift: ends slide in or stand\nup; the Mike walks up",
                          "snap: five on the line,\nthree hands down: a tite",
                          "four rush; the walked-up\nMike drops to the flat"],
                   rings=(("LE", style.DEFENSE), ("MIKE", style.THIRD)), lateral=(-10.6, 11.4),
                   window=(-8.4, 8.8), after=shift_marks, width_in=6.0, relabel=shift_label)
```

Why go to that trouble? Because, as [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) explained,
an offensive line decides its blocking before the snap: who is covered, who doubles, who climbs, and,
on a pass, which way the center slides and who picks up which rusher. A front that shifts at the last
moment makes those decisions against the wrong picture. In @fig-same-personnel-two-fronts the line set
its rules against a four-man even front with two linebackers; at the snap it faced a five-man line
with one, and on the pass, the player it had counted as a rusher (the walked-up Mike) was in coverage.
Notice what the shift does *not* do: it never puts a 250-pound edge rusher on a tackle's inside shoulder.
Every interior spot of the tite is still held by a defensive lineman; the only man who changes stance is
the end who stands up on the outside. Georgia's defense under Kirby Smart is known for exactly this
move, from a 4-2-5 into its mint front without a substitution: one tackle to the nose, the other tackle
and an end to 4is, the other end standing up and walking out.[^georgia]

The cost of being multiple is complexity. Every front has its own gap assignments and its own fits, and
every player has to know all of them; a shift that is a beat late leaves a gap empty at the snap. That
is why multiple defenses are built around smart, versatile players (edges who can rush and drop,
linemen who can play a 3 and a 4i) and why they live and die on the communication of the
[green-dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) linebacker who relays the call.

## Dialect: Okie, Eagle, G, and the problem with names

You now know what the fronts *are*. A word about what they are *called*, because front names are the
least standardized vocabulary in football. Every staff has a language, inherited from the coaches who
trained its coaches, and the same word can mean different things in neighbouring buildings. Two names
you will hear are good examples.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dialect
#| fig-cap: "Dialect, drawn against the Okie (left). Middle, the Eagle front as many modern 3-4 playbooks use the word: the ends pinch from the tackles' outside shoulders (5s) to their inside shoulders (4is), which is the same picture Fangio's staffs call tite and Kirby Smart's Georgia calls mint. Right, a G front: one letter in the call moves one man, the nose, off the center onto the guard's inside shoulder (a 2i, G for guard), here toward the tight end. Everyone else is where the Okie put him, but the center is now uncovered and has to step sideways to help on the nose. Dark dots are hands on the ground; the ringed players are the ones who moved."
DIALECT = [("Okie", [("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)], ()),
           ("Eagle (one dialect)", [("LE", "4i", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4i", 1)], ("LE", "RE")),
           ("G: nose on a guard", [("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "2i", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)], ("NT",))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
for ax, (ttl, spec, moved) in zip(axes, DIALECT):
    dfn = front(spec, lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.1, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 2.1, "M")],
                others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -6.2, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.2, "E")])
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in moved:
        p.highlight(k, color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.1, 8.3), window=(-4.6, 7.0), title=False)
    hands(f, p, ("LE", "NT", "RE"))
    if "G" in ttl:      # the uncovered center has to step sideways to reach the 2i
        point_to(f, p, (-3.2, -3.6), (-0.8, -0.2), "C now steps\nsideways", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
                 fontsize=6.5, shrink=5)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

**The [Eagle front](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eagle-front)** has meant at least three things.
In the 1940s it was Greasy Neale's five-man line, the Philadelphia Eagles' defense and the 3-4's
ancestor. In the late 1980s Fritz Shurmur, the Los Angeles Rams' defensive coordinator, built a
linebacker-heavy package he called the Eagle, and later wrote a coaching book on it, *The Eagle Five
Linebacker Defense* (1993). Its usual shape had only two down linemen, with five linebackers; in the
Rams' 21–7 playoff win over Philadelphia after the 1989 season, Shurmur went further, playing zone on
every snap and using five linebackers and six defensive backs, with no defensive linemen at all, on
long-yardage downs.[^shurmur] And in modern 3-4 playbooks, "Eagle" is a reduction, but staffs disagree
about which one. In some it is the Okie with *both* ends pinched inside to 4is: the middle panel of
@fig-dialect, the same alignment other staffs call tite or mint. In others it is a one-side change-up:
an outside linebacker walks up onto the tackle and the end beside him reduces inside to a 3, which is
the Under-like 3-4 of @fig-okie-two-ways.[^eaglemodern] Several meanings, one word, and only context
tells you which.

**The [G front](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-g-front)** is a tag rather than a whole front: it
moves the nose from the center (or from his shade on the center, in a four-man front) onto a guard's
inside shoulder, a 2i. "G" is for guard. It is a small move with a specific purpose. Inside zone's
first double team is usually the center and a guard on the nose, both stepping *forward* into him so
they can drive him back and then let one man climb to the linebacker. With the nose on the guard instead,
the center has to step *sideways* to reach him. A sideways step carries no push, so the double forms a
beat late and moves nobody, and by the time either blocker can come off it, the linebacker behind the
nose has already filled. You'll most often see the G tag on four-man
Over and Under fronts, where it moves a 1-technique to a 2i. The right panel of @fig-dialect borrows
the same move for the Okie to show what it does; whether a three-man front uses the letter G for it
varies by staff.[^gfront] Run the one-glance test on it, too: with the nose on a guard, nobody is head-up
on the center, so a G front is, by alignment, *even*, whatever the base defense is called. That is the
point of the tag. It changes who is covered.

Mint is the same kind of word: Georgia's name, under Kirby Smart, for the front Fangio's staffs call
tite. The point is not to memorize every staff's dictionary. It is to
read the *alignment* first and attach the name second. If an analyst says "Eagle" and you see 4is inside
the tackles, you know what he means even if his playbook and yours disagree.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, the defensive playbook is a menu of named fronts: pick "3-4 Odd" or "Nickel 3-3-5 Wide" and
the players run to their spots. Real defenses don't call a front from a menu so much as build it from
rules. The call names a front, a tag or two (a G, a slant, who is the edge), and a coverage, and each
player's alignment then depends on where the offense puts its tight end and its back, which side is the
wide side of the field, and whether the offense shifts. Two teams can call the same word and line up
differently, and the same team can call two different words and end up in the same alignment. The
names are shorthand for a set of instructions, and every staff writes its own.
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Houston Texans 2011–2012"}
**The scheme:** Wade Phillips's one-gap 3-4 in his first two seasons in Houston, the defense of the
Phillips-branch section above. Pick any 2012 game and watch J.J. Watt.

**What to notice:**

- The ends' alignment and first step. Watt often lines up on a tackle's outside shoulder, like an Okie
  end (he moved around, inside to a 3 or a 4i too), and then attacks the gap at the snap instead of
  controlling the man. Count how often his first step is
  across the line.
- What the outside linebackers do. On most passing downs, both are rushing; Phillips's 3-4 rushed four
  like any four-man front.
- How often the "3-4" looks like an Under front with a linebacker standing up. That is the one-gap 3-4
  of @fig-okie-two-ways in its natural habitat.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Denver Broncos, Super Bowl 50 (2015 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl 50, February 7, 2016, at Levi's Stadium: Denver 24, Carolina 10. Phillips,
now Denver's coordinator, had the league's top defense by yards allowed, and in the Super Bowl his two
stand-up edges, Von Miller and DeMarcus Ware, chased the league MVP, Cam Newton, all night. Miller was
the game's MVP, with 2.5 sacks and two forced fumbles; Malik Jackson fell on the first in the end zone for
Denver's first touchdown.[^sb50game]

**What to notice:** the edges. Before each snap, find Miller and Ware: standing, wide, often on
different sides from snap to snap. Watch whether they rush or drop (mostly rush), how they win around
the tackles with speed, and how, on Newton's scrambles and designed runs, they keep contain rather than
racing past him. When Denver goes to nickel, look for the 2-4-5 of this chapter: Miller and Ware stay
on the edges, standing or with a hand down, and the 3-4 has quietly become a four-man line. The stand-up
edge as a weapon is this game.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024"}
**The season:** Vic Fangio's first year as the Eagles' defensive coordinator. The defense allowed the
fewest yards in the NFL, about 278 a game, and the season ended with a 40–22 Super Bowl LIX win in which
the Eagles pressured Patrick Mahomes with four-man rushes.[^eagles24] Its five-man front was the tite of
this chapter, with Jordan Davis, a 341-pound nose at his combine, between two 4is, usually Jalen Carter
and Milton Williams, and two edges outside them.[^eaglesfront]

**What to notice:**

- Count the hands down on early downs. Three inside the tackles, with an edge on each side, is the tite.
- Watch Davis against a double team on an inside run: does the pair move him? Then find the linebacker
  behind him and see whether a blocker ever reaches him.
- Watch the safeties on those runs. They start deep, often 12 yards or more, and arrive late but fast.
  That is the light-box bargain: the front holds the line so the safeties can stay home on the pass.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Georgia 2021"}
**The season:** Kirby Smart's Georgia defense, which many observers rank among the best in college
football history, won the national championship, beating Alabama 33–18.[^georgia21] Its front featured two
interior linemen the Eagles later drafted in the first round, Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter, so the 2021
Bulldogs and the 2024 Eagles are, in a sense, the same front four years apart.

**What to notice:** the pre-snap movement. Smart's Georgia defenses are known for lining up in a
four-man front and shifting into mint, as in @fig-same-personnel-two-fronts, while the offense calls
its plays (the source for that move describes the scheme in 2025; watch whether the 2021 unit does it). Watch the offensive line's heads turn as the front changes, and then where the run goes.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap: count the hands, find the center.**

- Is anybody head-up on the center? A nose over the ball means an odd front; nobody there means an even
  one.
- Count the hands on the ground. Four is a four-man line, whatever the graphic says. Two down plus two
  standing edges is also a four-man line, usually a 3-4 team's 2-4-5 nickel. Three inside the tackles
  plus a standing edge on each side is a five-man tite (or mint) front.
- Who is standing on the edges? A standing edge is a rusher who might drop; note his number and watch
  him on passes.
- Where are the ends: outside the tackles (5s, built to beat the reach and set the edge), head-up (4s, two-gappers)
  or inside them (4is, a tite, built to choke inside runs)? From the high sideline camera, look at the
  two helmets: is the defender's helmet on the guard's side of the tackle's helmet, on top of it, or on
  the far side? If you can't tell, the end-zone replay angle (see Even Fronts) shows it at once.

**At the snap: the first step and the count.**

- Did the front change in the last seconds? A shift (an edge sliding inside, a linebacker walking up)
  means the defense is trying to beat the offensive line's blocking calls.
- Do the ends step into the tackles' chests (two-gap) or into the gaps (one-gap)?
- On a pass, how many rushed, and who? Five on the line rushing four means somebody standing at the line
  dropped.

**After the play: where did the run go?**

- Against a tite, did the inside run get through, or did it bounce outside? If it bounced, who made the
  tackle: an edge, the linebacker, or a safety?
- Did the offense's play fit the front? Inside zone into a tite is a fight on the defense's terms;
  outside zone and perimeter runs test its edges.

For your prediction log ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
on first and second down, write down the number of hands on the ground and whether the front was odd or
even, then whether the run went inside or outside. After a quarter you'll know which front the defense
uses to stop what, and whether the offense noticed.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Name it, then pick a run.** First-and-10 from the offense's own 35. The offense is in the
shotgun with three receivers and an attached tight end (Y). The defense is in nickel. Name the front.
How many defenders are in the box, and how many blockers does the offense have? If you were calling the
run, would you run inside zone, or something else?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: the defense's alignment before the snap (dark dots are hands on the ground). Two safeties deep, a nickel ($) over the slot on the left, and the corners on the wide receivers (outside the picture)."
off = gun11(y_attached=True)
dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
       D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")] + secondary(nickel_w=-6.2, high=11.5, safety_w=7.6)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: first-and-10, nickel")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-11.6, 11.6), window=(-7.0, 13.4))
hands(f, p, ("L4", "NT", "R4"))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A tite.** Three hands down inside the tackles (a 4i, a 0 and a 4i) with a stand-up edge on each side
make five on the line, and one linebacker stands behind them: the coach's 3-3-5, the Penny of the
Fangio tree.

**Six in the box against six blockers** (five linemen and the tight end), with two safeties deep and the
nickel outside the box. On paper that is a light box, and analysts will tell you to run against light
boxes. But this light box was *built* to be run into. Inside zone aims at the play-side B gap, where the
4i is; the nose and the 4is will occupy all five offensive linemen, and the Mike will fill his gap
unblocked, as in @fig-tite-inside-zone.

**The better calls test what the tite gives up.** Outside zone or a toss to the tight-end side attacks
the empty C gap: the right tackle is uncovered, so he can help the tight end on the edge or climb to the
only linebacker, and the Mike and the strong safety have to beat the ball to the alley. A run with the quarterback reading the backside edge (a zone read) turns the unblocked edge into
a wasted defender. Or don't run at all: a single linebacker in a light box is exactly the defender an
RPO or a quick throw underneath attacks. The defense has dared you to run inside; the smart offense
declines.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Choose your front.** You coordinate the defense. This week's opponent runs outside zone more
than any other play, from tight formations with the quarterback under center, and its tight end is an
excellent blocker. Here are two fronts you could show on first down. Which would you rather be in, and
where will the run most likely go against each?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: two fronts against the same under-center, one-tight-end formation. Front A: the tite: a 0 and two 4is between two stand-up edges, the right edge on the tight end's outside shoulder (a 9), one linebacker. Front B: a four-man even front aligned wide: a 3-technique on the right guard's outside shoulder, a 1 on the center, a 5 on the left tackle and a defensive end (9) on the tight end, with two linebackers."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
OFF_UC = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
fA = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
      D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")]
fB = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
           lbs=[("WILL", 4.7, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.7, 1.6, "M")])
for ax, dfn, hd, ttl in [(axes[0], fA, ("L4", "NT", "R4"), "Front A: tite"),
                         (axes[1], fB, ("LE", "L1", "R3", "RE"), "Front B: wide four-man")]:
    p = Play(OFF_UC, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.8), window=(-8.4, 6.8), title=False)
    hands(f, p, hd)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Front B is the better bet against this opponent, though neither is free.** Outside zone lives on reach
blocks. In Front B, the defenders on the play side are all *outside* the men who must reach them: the 3
outside the right guard, the end outside the tight end. Those are the hardest reaches in football, and a
quick 3-technique can be through the B gap before the guard gets there (the one-gap animation in
[Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)). If the reaches fail, the back can't get
outside and has to cut up early, into two linebackers.

In Front A, the trouble is the gap nobody is in. The play-side C gap, between the right tackle and the
tight end, is empty, so the right tackle is uncovered: he can help the tight end, an excellent blocker,
on the edge, or climb straight to the only linebacker. The 4i and the nose, big men built to hold
ground, have to chase the play sideways. Everything rests on one edge against two blockers, with one
linebacker and a safety coming from depth to fill the alley. Expect the ball to bounce outside if the
edge is reached, or to cut back if the Mike over-runs it.

**What Front B gives up:** the interior. Against the same team's *inside* zone, the 1 and the 3 can be
doubled and the doubles can climb to two linebackers. That is why defenses facing an outside-zone team
mix fronts by down and formation instead of living in one, and why the tite's teams widen their edges
(or switch to four-man fronts) against wide-zone offenses.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Which 3-4 is it?** Two snaps from the same 3-4 defense against the same formation, and the
linemen line up in exactly the same place both times: a nose head-up on the center and the ends head-up
on the tackles. The pictures freeze each snap a quarter-second after the ball moves. Where a lineman has
moved, a dashed outline shows where he started. For each snap, say whether the front is
playing two-gap or one-gap, and which linebackers you expect to be free.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the interior of two snaps, a quarter-second after the ball is snapped (the linebackers, behind them, are not shown). Both snaps started from the same alignment: a 0 and two 4s, each nose to nose with a blocker. Snap A: each lineman is still nose to nose with his blocker, hands on his chest (dark bars). Snap B: each lineman has stepped diagonally, all toward the tight end (arrows from the dashed outlines where they started), and is now in the seam beside his blocker."
STEPS3 = {False: {"LE": (0.72, -3.2), "NT": (0.72, 0.0), "RE": (0.72, 3.2)},
          True: {"LE": (0.62, -2.4), "NT": (0.62, 0.8), "RE": (0.62, 4.0)}}
START3 = {"LE": (1.0, -3.2), "NT": (1.0, 0.0), "RE": (1.0, 3.2)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.0, 4.6))
for ax, snapB in [(axes[0], False), (axes[1], True)]:
    dfn = front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
                others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -6.2, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.2, "E")])
    dfn = [q.moved(d=STEPS3[snapB][q.key][0], w=STEPS3[snapB][q.key][1]) if q.key in START3 else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.0), window=(-2.0, 2.8), title=False, width_in=6.0)
    for k, (d0, w0) in START3.items():
        d1, w1 = STEPS3[snapB][k]
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(f, p, d0, w0), _P(f, p, d1, w1)
        if snapB:   # where he started (dashed) and the step that took him into the gap
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((float(x0), float(y0)), 4, radius=0.94, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.6)), zorder=6))
            (xe, ye) = _P(f, p, d0 + 0.62 * (d1 - d0), w0 + 0.62 * (w1 - w0))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(xe), float(ye)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=12, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.8, zorder=13))
        else:       # hands on the blocker's chest
            (xc, yc), (xd, yd) = _P(f, p, 0.06, w1 - 0.6), _P(f, p, 0.06, w1 + 0.6)
            ax.plot([float(xc), float(xd)], [float(yc), float(yd)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=5.0,
                    solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=12)
    ax.set_title("Snap A" if not snapB else "Snap B", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Snap A is two-gap.** The alignment couldn't tell you, but the first step can: each lineman has stepped
straight *into* the blocker in front of him and put his hands on his chest, about to lock out and read.
That means three linemen are holding six gaps, the edge on the tight end has the D gap, and **both inside
linebackers are free**: they have no gap of their own at the snap and will read and fill wherever the
ball goes. If the linemen win, nobody blocks either of them.

**Snap B is one-gap**, from the same head-up alignment. Every lineman has slanted *into a gap* beside his
blocker, all toward the tight end: the left end into the B gap, the nose into the A gap toward the tight
end, the right end into the C gap. Every lineman has one gap, so the linebackers have one each too: the
Mike the B gap toward the tight end, the Will the other A gap, exactly the assignments of the right half
of @fig-okie-two-ways. **Nobody is free**, but everybody is fast. One-gap teams usually line up shaded,
as in that figure, but plenty of them line up head-up and slant, precisely so that the alignment gives
nothing away. That is why the first step, not the alignment, is the tell.
:::
:::

## Back to the broadcast

The chapter opened with a graphic that said 3-4 and a picture that kept changing. Now you can read both.

- *The graphic says 3-4, and you count four on the line, two standing*: that is the 3-4 team's
  **2-4-5 nickel**, its nose on the bench and its two outside linebackers on the edges. The roster says
  2-4-5; the football is a four-man line.
- *Next snap, five across the line, three of them enormous and wedged inside the tackles, one linebacker
  behind them*: a **tite**, built by sending the nose back on for a linebacker, the coach's 3-3-5. A
  **multiple** defense like Georgia's can reach the same picture without substituting at all, by shifting
  a four-man line into it at the last moment.
- *The inside run into a wall, the linebacker never touched*: the tite's whole purpose. A nose and two 4is
  occupy all five offensive linemen, the doubles can't climb, and the one linebacker fills his gap
  unblocked and makes the tackle.
  That is how six defenders stop a run aimed at six blockers: one of them, the nose, is doing the work of
  two.

## Takeaways

- **Find the center.** A defender head-up on the center makes the front odd; nobody there makes it even.
  The odd fronts are built around a heavy nose who takes two blockers so somebody else can run free.
- **The 3-4 Okie is one alignment played two ways.** Two-gap (head-up, control and read) keeps the inside
  linebackers clean at the cost of rare bodies and little pass rush; one-gap (shaded, attack) turns the
  3-4 into an aggressive front, often an Under with a standing Sam. The first step tells you which.
- **The stand-up edge is the 3-4's great legacy.** Standing gives him vision, width and the option to
  drop, which makes the defense's rush uncertain; the price is leverage against the run.
- **The tite walls off the middle.** A 0 and two 4is leave the offense's uncovered linemen stuck on
  doubles that can neither move them nor climb, so a light box with two safeties deep can still stop
  inside runs; the one linebacker owns the last gap, unblocked. It gives up pass rush, the perimeter
  (an empty C gap against outside zone) and the space underneath.
- **Fronts choose what to stop.** Line up on or inside blockers to beat double teams (inside runs); line up
  outside them, with every outside gap filled, to beat reaches (outside zone). No front does both, so defenses change fronts by opponent,
  by situation and by shifting at the snap.
- **Nickel labels are roster labels.** As roster counts, 4-2-5, 2-4-5 and 3-3-5 describe nearly the same
  box count and pass rush; what differs is whether the edges are listed as ends or linebackers. (When a
  coach *calls* a 3-3-5, he means the tite.) Count hands, not
  names, and read alignment before dialect.

**See also (case study):** [Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd),
the tite front and the light box as the run-defense half of the two-high era.

**If you want to go deeper:** Cody Alexander's *MatchQuarters* site and books (defensive structure,
including the tite and four-down fronts, from a coach's view); Chris B. Brown's *The Art of Smart Football*
and his Grantland and Smart Football writing on the 3-4 and its noses; and the 2024 Eagles' or 2021 Georgia
Bulldogs' games, watched for nothing but the three men inside the tackles.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Measuring the wall.** The tite's promise is that nobody climbs: every offensive lineman is still engaged
with a defensive lineman a second after the snap, so the linebacker behind them is untouched. Tracking data
can test that. A simple measure is the distance from the linebacker to the nearest offensive blocker:
two players whose centres are about a yard apart are in contact, so anything under about 1.5 yards means a
blocker has reached him. Here it is at three moments for the Mike in the simulated tite play above, and,
for contrast, for the Mike in the same inside zone against a four-man front that leaves the play-side
guard uncovered (a 1 on the center and a 3 on the left guard), so that the guard can climb. Both are
computed from Big Data Bowl-format frames (simulated, BDB-format):

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (nearest blocker to the linebacker, from tracking frames)"
def nearest_blocker(play, key, times=(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)):
    trk = play.to_tracking()
    me = trk[trk.displayName == key].set_index("time")
    ol = trk[trk.displayName.isin(OL_KEYS + ("Y",))]
    out = {}
    for t in times:
        m = me.loc[round(t, 1)]
        o = ol[ol.time.round(1) == round(t, 1)]
        out[f"+{t:.1f} s"] = f"{np.hypot(o.x - m.x, o.y - m.y).min():.1f} yd"
    return out


def even_iz():
    """Inside zone right against a four-man front: 3 on the left guard, 1 on the center's right shoulder,
    5s on the tackles. The right guard is uncovered: he helps on the 1, then climbs to the Mike."""
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "5"), D("L3", "DL", 1.0, T("3", -1), "3"),
           D("R1", "DL", 1.0, T("1", 1), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", 1), "5"),
           D("WILL", "LB", 4.7, -1.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 1.6, "M")]
    p = Play(gun11(y_attached=True), dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.35, 0.0), speed=1.4); go_to(p, "R1", (0.9, 0.9), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.2, 1.2), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "RG", (2.9, 1.9), speed=3.2)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 2.2), "path", speed=2.2, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "LG", (-0.3, -2.0), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "RT", (-0.3, 3.4), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 1.5), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-4.7, -0.2), (-3.8, 1.0)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.5)
    return p


as_markdown(pd.DataFrame([{"defender": "Mike vs inside zone, tite (simulated)", **nearest_blocker(P_TITE, "MIKE")},
                          {"defender": "Mike vs inside zone, uncovered guard (simulated)",
                           **nearest_blocker(even_iz(), "MIKE")}]))
```

Read the rows across. The tite's Mike closes on the line of scrimmage because he is filling, yet no
blocker ever gets within reach of him; against the uncovered guard, the distance shrinks toward the
1.5-yard line and then falls below a yard, which is the guard arriving on him. On real frames the same measure,
computed for every inside linebacker on every run, separates fronts that keep linebackers clean from
fronts that don't. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9)
has tracking for every player and a players file with positions; pair it with the nflverse participation
data above to tag each snap's front. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this cell is not run when the
book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
runs = plays[plays["isDropback"] == False]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
if "position" not in trk:
    trk = trk.merge(players, on="nflId", how="left")

OL = {"T", "G", "C"}
out = []
for g, pl in runs[["gameId", "playId"]].itertuples(index=False):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl, label="position")
    at1 = one[one["time"].round(1) == 1.0]
    lbs, ol = at1[at1["position"].isin(["ILB", "MLB"])], at1[at1["position"].isin(OL)]
    for r in lbs.itertuples():
        out.append({"gameId": g, "playId": pl, "nflId": r.nflId,
                    "nearest_ol": float(np.hypot(ol.x - r.x, ol.y - r.y).min())})
clean = pd.DataFrame(out)
(clean.nearest_ol > 1.5).mean()   # share of inside-linebacker run snaps with no blocker within 1.5 yards at 1 s
```
